United Nations and NATO said it was a good treaty, and that it was a treaty of reconciliation. Both of these things are true. As a treaty, one could say it is a model. It is generous, indeed much more generous to the defeated foe than it is to many of the allies of the victorious nations. It is a treaty which is not vindictive. It is a treaty which demands no reparations amounting to any sizeable sum. It is a treaty which imposes no restraint upon the sovereignty, no restraint upon the economic life, of Japan, yet there seems to be something fundamentally wrong with that treaty judging from the reaction of the people of Asia. The reason something is wrong with it is not in the treaty itself but in the fact that, rightly or wrongly, the people of Asia are convinced that this treaty does nothing else but make Japan an outpost for United States policy in the cold war. Nothing could be more regrettable.
The minister stated he hoped that this treaty would write a new chapter in the history of the Pacific. I should like to think so too, but I fear our hopes are doomed to frustration. The trouble really is that while the United States with great single-mindedness of purpose is engaged in a struggle against communism, so many people in Asia are engaged in the struggle against poverty. They do not share the United States ideas as to who is the real enemy. We have the situation in Australia, the Philippines, Indonesia and New Zealand where these countries have the strongest of reservations about a rearmed Japan. On this continent we are much more worried about Stalin and what he does than about what we want to do ourselves. So long as that situation obtains we are not going to be able to suggest constructive and progressive policies.
Some time ago General MacArthur said that the democratization-that is a word which I dislike-of Japan had been accomplished. Yet to me, and to many much more competent observers, the facts are that the forces of the old Japan are gathering together again in administrative positions. Today we see men in office whose thinking is precisely the same as that of Tojo. When we are asked to believe that Japan has gone through its purge and has become a new and shining democratic state, reason is strained to the point of rupture and I cannot accept it.
This afternoon the minister stated he hoped Japan would not turn to the trade practices which we had seen in the past. We all share that hope. Yet the fact is that a nation has to live. When a nation feels that its very existence is at stake, whatever laws are in the books are torn up. These are the facts which we must bear in mind. The pressures which in 1931 caused Japan to start on its career of


aggression are mounting. During the 1930's the Japanese population increased by a million extra mouths every year. Today she has a population of some 83 million human beings contained on three islands which, for all practical purposes, are poor and barren lands. In the next fifteen years Japan will have to absorb into industry some 8 million who are today children or babes in arms. The Japanese are going to find that their need for markets in this decade is going to be just as acute as the need for markets in the past. They have to get foreign markets. Are we in Canada going to welcome cheap Japanese imports?	Are the people of the United
States going to welcome cheap Japanese imports?	Are the people of the United
Kingdom? I doubt it very much. That being so, Japan will have to find some area with which she can trade and to which she can export.
The minister said the treaty does not bear the seeds of a future war, and that is true of the treaty itself. What might bear the seeds of a future war is the economic stupidity of the nations of the west. The fact is that Japan, whether we like it or not, is going to trade with China. After all, the industries of Japan were geared to Chinese raw materials. Today China will accept with gratitude any manufactured goods and machines which Japan can export. Indeed the Prime Minister of Japan, Mr. Yoshida, said recently:
In some quarters fear is entertained that a separate peace might permanently sever Japan's trade with Red China. Red or white, China remains our next-door neighbour. Geography and economic law, will, I believe, prevail in the long run over any ideological differences and artificial trade barriers.
These are words worth thinking about. It is true that, for the time being, we can expect Japan to support the policy of the United States; but I suspect it will only support it until that day comes when it has achieved independence. Japan knows very well that the United States needs it. Japan knows very well that it was Mr. Dulles who, despite what was written in the constitution about no more arms, insisted that Japan should rearm. I believe it was Mr. Yoshida who insisted that if Japan were to rearm, then the United States would have to do it. This would leave Japanese industry free to compete still further with other nations, the logical outcome in a world of power politics. Japan cannot afford to rearm herself because taxes are already high, the cost of living is rising and the standard of living is falling. By devoting a large amount of production to armament very serious unrest would be

caused in Japan, which perhaps would cause an incident such as we saw at Mukden some time ago.
What might conceivably happen, and what I believe will happen unless there is a tremendous change in philosophy amongst the governments of the west, is that Japan will very skilfully play the west off against China and Russia, attempting to get the best of both worlds. The picture I draw, the blueprint I sketch, may be rather pessimistic but I believe it is one which will prove to be reasonably accurate unless we change our way of working.
Now, why does Asia so strongly suspect the United States and the western powers? I believe the reason is that the people of the United States, by and large, do not seem to have realized that in their fight against communism they are aligning themselves with every group which is opposed to social and economic change. As a result we are all going to suffer, because the impression is that the west stands against something whereas we have got to stand for something. Now, what about the present danger? The minister himself suggested that it was not as serious as it had been some time ago. He suggested that it was still serious, heaven knows, but not as acute as it had been, and not as bad as in 1948 when the economies of Europe were on the verge of cracking and the communist parties were growing in almost every country on that continent. Indeed, it was so bad in 1948 that some commentators could almost forecast the entry of soviet troops into western Europe. Today we are stronger. Today we are told by the minister-and it is true-the morale of Europe is high. Today the fear of aggression is somewhat less. Yet at this time when Europe is getting back on its feet there is this request by the United States that there must be a still further effort at rearmament. In view of what the Europeans have done, it is possible that if further rearmament is to be imposed upon them it is going to come into violent collision with social and economic realities. Indeed Mr. Paul Hoffman recognized that in his book "Peace Can Be Won" when he said at page 111:
. . . too great a pressure for rearming on a nation of full employment, like Britain, could unduly drive down the standard of living . . .
That is the very thing Europe fears; because if we depress their standard of living far enough, as my leader said this afternoon, we play completely into the hands of the communists. Mr. Kent Cooper, the executive director of the Associated Press, said on July 30 of this year that Europe is frightened of United States defence pressure. Europe is 94699-19
United Nations and NATO frightened of other things. Europe is frightened of Soviet aggression, but today that fear is not quite so great as it was, although it is just as real.
I have not altered my views at all. The men of the Kremlin believe that war is inevitable between east and west; therefore we must prepare for that eventuality. But it is not beyond the bounds of possibility that these same men believe they can win the war without fighting. They may suggest peace programs which have been described so correctly as being phony. There are some who think that soviet diplomacy over the years has been skilful, not to say Machiavellian. I think that basically and fundamentally soviet foreign policy, if it tjesired to achieve its ends, has been stupid; for obviously what would have served the soviet rulers much better than having full employment in the western world is a depression and the hopelessness that comes from it.
The economic indications of a year ago last spring were interesting. Had one made a graph of the unemployment figures in Canada in each spring since 1946, one would have seen that they were steadily rising until in 1950 they had reached the critical stage, indicating that 7 or 8 per cent of our working population were unemployed. One could see the same thing in the United States; and there was no answer to the problem of unemployment until Korea. We now find ourselves with full employment, with a prosperity which I fear is synthetic but which has completely destroyed Russia's hope of conquering us by throwing us into a depression. Yet despite these lessons of the past can we say that we have really presented to the world a creative, progressive idea for which men will fight and die? I do not think that is the case; and until it comes about we are not going to be victors in any war, be it cold or be it hot.
I have here a copy of the July issue of "External Affairs", in which is reported a speech that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) gave at Northwestern university. One may say: here is the idea for which men are groping. The Prime Minister said:
A defensive effort designed; only to safeguard the material and moral advantages enjoyed by the inhabitants of this continent and of western Europe will not give us the security we want.
There can be no objection to that sentence, which is true. The next sentence is:
It is the essential first step.
That is true. The Prime Minister then continued:
But if we hope to provide enduring safeguards of those moral and material advantages we must, in a true spirit of equality and co-operation, join

United Nations and NATO
with the less favoured areas of the world in a concerted effort to give their inhabitants greater material advantages and greater hopes for the future.
Again, that is profoundly true; but still it is only words. It is true that we are going to give $25 million to the Colombo plan. It is a start which we welcome. But we do not yet know how much is going to follow. I echo the hope of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that the government will make it amply clear that we are going to play our full part in the six-year program. Then the Prime Minister went on to say: Some of you are probably asking yourself: When can we hope to get back to normal? When can we return to living decent American lives without having to worry about the problems of the rest of the human race? Well, I am afraid the answer to those questions is: Not in my day nor in yours.
When I read those remarks, it was first of all with approval. I read them again, more critically; then I saw the gulf which seems to separate the thinking of members of the government from that of the C.C.F. When can we hope to get back to normal? What is normal? Were conditions normal in 1946, when we were emerging from the throes of war? Can one say that 1939 was normal with its tens of thousands of unemployed who had to wait until war came in order to find work? Were times normal in the depths of the depression in 1932 and 1933? Or were times normal in 1929 when we had in this country
a false prosperity which burst like a pricked balloon? Is there any such thing as normal times? I suggest there is not. I believe it is really a waste of time to look backward toward those times instead of looking toward the future.
Then, "when can we return to living decent American lives without having to worry about the problems of the rest of the human race?" My answer to that question is "Never" because I think we are morally bound to worry about the problems of the rest of the human race. I believe that we are our brothers' keepers.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we shall continue the debate on this motion. Then we shall proceed with the resolution to amend the Railway Act; then the second reading of Bill No. 6, to amend the Canadian National-Canadian Pacific Act, 1933; then if we have more time, we will take Bill No. 7, to amend the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to the order of the house passed on October 12, 1951.
